claim: The GARP complex functions in endosome-to-Golgi retrograde vesicular transport.
source: the Golgi-associated retrograde protein (GARP) complex, which functions in endosome-to-Golgi retrograde vesicular transport, as a critical player in sphingolipid homeostasis
evidence: This is stated as an established function of the GARP complex in the abstract, drawing on existing scientific knowledge about this protein complex.

claim: GARP deficiency leads to accumulation of sphingolipid synthesis intermediates.
source: GARP deficiency leads to accumulation of sphingolipid synthesis intermediates, changes in sterol distribution, and lysosomal dysfunction
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including lipidomic analyses showing increased long-chain bases in GARP mutants.

claim: GARP deficiency leads to changes in sterol distribution.
source: GARP deficiency leads to accumulation of sphingolipid synthesis intermediates, changes in sterol distribution, and lysosomal dysfunction
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including filipin staining and lipidomic analyses showing altered sterol distribution in GARP mutants.

claim: GARP deficiency leads to lysosomal dysfunction.
source: GARP deficiency leads to accumulation of sphingolipid synthesis intermediates, changes in sterol distribution, and lysosomal dysfunction
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing vacuolar fragmentation and altered lysosome morphology in GARP-deficient cells.

claim: A GARP complex mutation analogous to a VPS53 allele causing PCCA2 in humans exhibits similar, albeit weaker, phenotypes in yeast.
source: A GARP complex mutation analogous to a VPS53 allele causing progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy type 2 (PCCA2) in humans exhibits similar, albeit weaker, phenotypes in yeast
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the vps53 Q624R mutant phenotypes to vps53Δ deletion phenotypes in yeast.

claim: Inhibition of the first step of de novo sphingolipid synthesis is sufficient to mitigate many of the phenotypes of GARP-deficient yeast or mammalian cells.
source: Inhibition of the first step of de novo sphingolipid synthesis is sufficient to mitigate many of the phenotypes of GARP-deficient yeast or mammalian cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that myriocin treatment suppresses growth defects, vacuolar fragmentation, and other phenotypes in GARP mutants.

claim: GARP is essential for cellular sphingolipid homeostasis.
source: these data show that GARP is essential for cellular sphingolipid homeostasis
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing sphingolipid imbalances and accumulation of intermediates in GARP-deficient cells.

claim: Sphingolipids make up between 10 and 20% of the mammalian plasma membrane.
source: Sphingolipids make up between 10 and 20% of the mammalian plasma membrane (van Meer et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Meer et al., 2008.

claim: Sphingolipids are generated in the ER and Golgi.
source: They are generated in the ER and Golgi and are subsequently delivered to the plasma membrane by vesicular transport
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Klemm et al., 2009 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Sphingolipids are delivered to the plasma membrane by vesicular transport.
source: They are generated in the ER and Golgi and are subsequently delivered to the plasma membrane by vesicular transport (Klemm et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Klemm et al., 2009.

claim: Sphingolipids at the plasma membrane are internalized by endocytosis and delivered to the lysosome for catabolism.
source: Sphingolipids at the plasma membrane are internalized by endocytosis and delivered to the lysosome for catabolism
evidence: This represents established knowledge about sphingolipid trafficking and metabolism.

claim: Sphingolipids can be recycled from endocytic vesicles back to the plasma membrane via the Golgi apparatus.
source: Sphingolipids can also be recycled from endocytic vesicles back to the plasma membrane via the Golgi apparatus (Choudhury et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Choudhury et al., 2002.

claim: Ceramide and sphingosine-1-phosphate are important signaling molecules that mediate cell proliferation, differentiation, and death.
source: intermediates of sphingolipid synthesis, including ceramide and sphingosine-1-phosphate, are important signaling molecules that mediate cell proliferation, differentiation, and death
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hannun and Obeid, 2008; Maceyka and Spiegel, 2014; Montefusco et al., 2014.

claim: A reduction in plasma membrane sphingolipid levels results in activation of the Ypk1/2 kinases through the TORC2-signaling cascade in yeast.
source: In yeast, a reduction in plasma membrane sphingolipid levels results in activation of the Ypk1/2 kinases through the TORC2-signaling cascade (Roelants et al., 2011; Berchtold et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roelants et al., 2011 and Berchtold et al., 2012.

claim: Orm1/2 proteins are negative regulators of serine-palmitoyl transferase (SPT).
source: Substrates of these kinases, the ER-localized Orm1/2 proteins, are negative regulators of serine-palmitoyl transferase (SPT), an enzyme that catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of sphingolipid synthesis (Breslow et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Breslow et al., 2010.

claim: SPT catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of sphingolipid synthesis.
source: serine-palmitoyl transferase (SPT), an enzyme that catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of sphingolipid synthesis
evidence: This represents established knowledge in sphingolipid metabolism.

claim: The phosphorylation of Orm1/2 releases these proteins from SPT, thereby initiating sphingolipid synthesis.
source: The phosphorylation of Orm1/2 releases these proteins from SPT, thereby initiating sphingolipid synthesis and the generation of the early synthesis intermediates, long-chain bases
evidence: This is supported by citation to Breslow et al., 2010 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Ypk1/2 kinases phosphorylate key subunits of ceramide synthase, increasing its activity.
source: Ypk1/2 kinases phosphorylate key subunits of the sphingolipid metabolic enzyme ceramide synthase, increasing its activity and flux of more distal steps of sphingolipid biosynthesis (Muir et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Muir et al., 2014.

claim: Lysosomal storage diseases such as Niemann-Pick type C and Gaucher's disease result from lysosomal accumulation of different sphingolipid species.
source: a number of lysosomal storage diseases, such as Niemann–Pick type C or Gaucher's disease, result from lysosomal accumulation of different sphingolipid species (Platt, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Platt, 2014.

claim: Lysosomal storage diseases preferentially affect the central nervous system.
source: These diseases preferentially affect the central nervous system (Platt, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Platt, 2014.

claim: Sphingolipid imbalance can lead to neurotoxicity.
source: suggesting that sphingolipid imbalance can lead to neurotoxicity
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that lysosomal storage diseases preferentially affect the central nervous system.

claim: The GARP complex and retromer were identified as strong suppressors in a genome-wide chemical genetic screen with myriocin.
source: One of the strongest class of suppressors identified in the screen (p < 10−7) contained factors mediating retrograde trafficking from endosomes to the Golgi (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This included mutants in each subunit of the GARP complex (vps51Δ, vps52Δ, vps53Δ, and vps54Δ) and in four of five subunits of retromer
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the genome-wide screen showing statistical significance.

claim: The GARP complex is strongly enriched among the suppressor mutants identified in the myriocin screen (p < 10−5).
source: Note, the GARP complex is strongly enriched among the suppressor mutants identified (p < 10−5)
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Golgi complex is not enriched among the suppressor mutants identified in the myriocin screen (p > 10−3).
source: whereas the Golgi complex is not (p > 10−3)
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GARP mutants are sensitive to IPC synthase inhibition by aureobasidin A.
source: GARP mutants are sensitive to IPC synthase inhibition. Wild-type, vps51Δ, vps52Δ, vps53Δ, and vps54Δ cells were spotted on control plates and plates containing 0.05 μM aureobasidin A
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating growth defects of GARP mutants on aureobasidin A plates.

claim: GARP mutants are sensitive to ceramide synthase inhibition by fumonisin B1.
source: GARP mutants are sensitive to ceramide synthase inhibition. Wild-type, vps51Δ, vps52Δ, vps53Δ, and vps54Δ cells were spotted on control plates and plates containing 100 μM fumonisin B1
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating growth defects of GARP mutants on fumonisin B1 plates.

claim: VPS53 mutants are sensitive to overexpression of the alkaline ceramidase Ypc1.
source: VPS53 mutants are sensitive to overexpression of the alkaline ceramidase Ypc1. Wild-type or vps53Δ cells harboring an empty plasmid or a plasmid encoding YPC1 under control of the GAL10 promoter were spotted on glucose- or galactose-containing plates
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating growth defects of vps53Δ mutants overexpressing Ypc1.

claim: GARP mutants are sensitive to high levels of long-chain bases, specifically phytosphingosine (PHS).
source: GARP mutants are sensitive to high levels of long-chain bases, early sphingolipid intermediates. Wild-type, vps53Δ, and vps54Δ cells were spotted on control plates or plates containing 30 μM phytosphingosine (PHS)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D demonstrating growth defects of GARP mutants on PHS-containing plates.

claim: GARP complex deficiency results in an accumulation of long-chain bases.
source: GARP complex deficiency results in an accumulation of long-chain bases. The lipidomic analysis of sphingolipids from vps53Δ (black) compared with wild-type strains (white) is shown
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 2E demonstrating increased long-chain base levels in vps53Δ cells.

claim: vps53Δ cells showed an eightfold increase in levels of total long-chain bases compared with wild-type controls.
source: Strikingly, vps53Δ cells showed an eightfold increase in levels of total long-chain bases compared with wild-type controls (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative lipidomic data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Dihydrosphingosine (DHS) increased approximately tenfold in vps53Δ cells.
source: Among the different long-chain base species, dihydrosphingosine (DHS) increased ∼tenfold
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Phytosphingosine (PHS) increased approximately threefold in vps53Δ cells.
source: PHS increased ∼threefold (Figure 2F,G)
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: vps53Δ cells had a twofold reduction of the complex sphingolipid M(IP)2C.
source: In addition, vps53Δ cells had a ∼twofold reduction of the complex sphingolipid M(IP)2C (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The levels of IPC, MIPC, and ceramides were unchanged in vps53Δ cells.
source: the levels of IPC, MIPC, and ceramides were unchanged
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data analysis.

claim: Orm1 was hyperphosphorylated in vps53Δ cells compared with controls.
source: Consistent with this model, we found that Orm1 was hyperphosphorylated in vps53Δ cells compared with controls (Figure 2H)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Myriocin treatment greatly reduced the accumulation of long-chain bases in GARP mutants.
source: Importantly, myriocin treatment greatly reduced the accumulation of long-chain bases in each of the GARP mutants (Figure 2F,G)
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: The rate of long-chain base decrease during myriocin treatment was similar in wild-type and vps53Δ cells.
source: The rate of long-chain base decrease during the myriocin treatment time course was similar in wild-type and vps53Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: After prolonged myriocin treatment, DHS levels remained elevated in GARP mutants compared with untreated control cells.
source: However, even after prolonged, DHS levels remained elevated compared with untreated control cells, suggesting the pool of long-chain bases turns over more slowly (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 2F and represents an inference about turnover rates.

claim: Sphingolipid recycling remains blocked upon myriocin treatment in GARP mutants.
source: Sphingolipid recycling remains blocked upon myriocin treatment and sphingolipids accumulate in vacuoles
evidence: This is supported by NBD-sphingosine staining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sphingolipids accumulate in vacuoles in vps53Δ cells.
source: Sphingolipid recycling remains blocked upon myriocin treatment and sphingolipids accumulate in vacuoles. Wild-type cells (top panels), wild-type cells treated with myriocin (1 μM, 12hr), vps53Δ cells, or vps53Δ cells treated with myriocin (1 μM, 12hr). NBD-sphingosine, green. Vacuoles (FM4-64), red
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating NBD-sphingosine accumulation in FM4-64 labeled vacuoles.

claim: Inhibition of sphingolipid biosynthesis partially restores vacuolar morphology in GARP mutants.
source: Inhibition of sphingolipid biosynthesis partially restores vacuolar morphology in GARP mutants
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3B and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Three targets of zinc transcription factor Zap1 (Adh4, Zrt1, Zps1) are down regulated in the GARP mutant vps53Δ.
source: Three targets of zinc transcription factor Zap1 are down regulated in the GARP mutant vps53Δ. A proteomic analysis of vps53Δ and wild-type cells is shown. Protein intensities are plotted against light/heavy SILAC ratios. Significant outliers are colored in red (P < 1−11)
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GARP mutant zinc sensitivity is rescued by myriocin treatment.
source: GARP mutant zinc sensitivity is rescued by myriocin treatment. Wild-type and vps53Δ cells were spotted on control plates or plates containing 1 μM myriocin, 4 mM zinc or 1 μM myriocin and 4 mM zinc
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Intracellular sterols accumulate in the GARP mutants vps53Δ and vps54Δ.
source: Intracellular sterols accumulate in the GARP mutants vps53Δ and vps54Δ. Wild-type (left panels), vps53Δ cells (middle panels), and vps54Δ cell (right panels) treated with methanol (top panels) or myriocin (lower panels) were stained with filipin
evidence: This is supported by filipin staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neutral lipids accumulate in the GARP mutant vps53Δ.
source: Neutral lipids accumulate in the GARP mutant vps53Δ. Lipidomic analysis of neutral lipids isolated from vps53Δ (black) expressed in fold change from the wild-type (white)
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: vps53Δ mutants showed a two to threefold increase in ergosterol esters.
source: However, we detected a two to threefold increase in ergosterol esters in these cells
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: vps53Δ mutants showed a threefold increase in lipid droplets per cell compared with wild-type cells.
source: Consistent with this, vps53Δ mutants showed a threefold increase in lipid droplets per cell, as identified by the LD marker protein Faa4, compared with wild-type cells (Figure 4C,D)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: VPS52 shows synthetic growth defects with mutations in several genes encoding enzymes of ergosterol biosynthesis (ERG2, ERG20, ERG25, ERG26).
source: we analyzed genetic interaction data (Hoppins et al., 2011) of vps52Δ and found synthetic growth defects with mutations in several genes encoding enzymes of ergosterol biosynthesis (ERG2, ERG20, ERG25, ERG26) (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is supported by E-MAP genetic interaction data shown in Figure 4E and cited from Hoppins et al., 2011.

claim: VPS52 showed positive correlations with many genes in ergosterol metabolism (ERG3, ERG25, ERG26, ERG6, ERG2, and ERG4).
source: In addition, VPS52 showed positive correlations with many genes in ergosterol metabolism (ERG3, ERG25, ERG26, ERG6, ERG2, and ERG4; Figure 4F)
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Compound heterozygous mutations of human VPS53 cause progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy type 2 (PCCA2).
source: Compound heterozygous mutations of human VPS53 cause progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy type 2 (PCCA2) (Feinstein et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feinstein et al., 2014.

claim: A mutation analogous to the VPS53 allele causing PCCA2 in humans is partially resistant to sphingolipid biosynthesis inhibition induced by myriocin.
source: A mutation analogous to the VPS53 allele causing progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy type 2 (PCCA2) in humans is partially resistant to sphingolipid biosynthesis inhibition induced by myriocin
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Endosome-Golgi trafficking is partially impaired in yeast cells expressing the analogous PCCA2-causing mutation vps53 Q624R.
source: Endosome-Golgi trafficking is partially impaired in yeast cells expressing the analogous PCCA2-causing mutation vps53 Q624R
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B demonstrating altered Vps10-GFP localization.

claim: The CPY receptor Vps10 accumulates in vps53 Q624R endosomes.
source: The CPY receptor Vps10 accumulates in vps53 Q624R endosomes. Quantification of the distribution of Vps10-GFP between the Sec7-decorated Golgi (white bars) and retromer-decorated endosomes (black bars) in wild-type and vps53 Q624R cells
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cells harboring a vps53 Q624R mutant allele had significantly reduced Vps10 levels in the Golgi apparatus (28%, compared with 43% in wild-type cells).
source: Using this assay, we found that cells harboring a vps53 Q624R mutant allele had significantly reduced Vps10 levels in the Golgi apparatus (28%, compared with 43% in wild-type cells)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cells harboring a vps53 Q624R mutant allele had increased Vps10 signal in the endosome (49%, compared with 24% in wild-type cells).
source: and increased signal in the endosome (49%, compared with 24% in wild-type cells; Figure 5C)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: vps53 Q624R mutant cells showed vacuolar fragmentation, which was found three times more frequently than in control cells (33% vs 11%).
source: Also consistent with a partial loss of GARP function, vps53 Q624R mutant cells showed vacuolar fragmentation, highlighted by multiple small vacuoles in cells, which we found three times more frequently than in control cells (33% vs 11%, Figure 5D,E)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Knock-down of VPS53 in HeLa cells results in accumulation of free cholesterol.
source: Similar to our findings in yeast, knock-down of the VPS53 subunit of the GARP complex in HeLa cells resulted in accumulation of free cholesterol
evidence: This is supported by filipin staining data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Myriocin treatment reduced build-up of free cholesterol due to GARP complex deficiency in HeLa cells.
source: Myriocin treatment reduced build-up of free cholesterol due to GARP complex deficiency. Filipin staining of unesterified cholesterol in control (top panels) or Vps53 knock-down (lower panels) in HeLa cells treated with 1 μM myriocin for 12 hr (right panels) or DMSO as a control (left panels)
evidence: This is supported by filipin staining data shown in Figure 6A and quantification in Figure 6B.

claim: Lysosomes appeared swollen and clustered in the juxtanuclear area of Vps53 knock-down cells.
source: We confirmed that lysosomes appeared swollen and clustered in the juxtanuclear area of Vps53 knock-down cells
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Myriocin treatment resulted in a more uniform lysosome distribution and partially reduced the size of LAMP-1 positive lysosomes in Vps53 knock-down cells.
source: Importantly, myriocin treatment resulted in a more uniform lysosome distribution and partially reduced the size of LAMP-1 positive lysosomes in Vps53 knock-down cells (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: VPS53 knock-down in HeLa cells resulted in a 2.5 fold increase in hexosylceramide.
source: We found a ∼2.5 fold increase in hexosylceramide
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: VPS53 knock-down in HeLa cells resulted in a significant increase in the levels of sphingosine and sphinganine.
source: and a significant increase in the levels of sphingosine and sphinganine
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: VPS53 knock-down in HeLa cells resulted in a decrease in sphingomyelin.
source: as well as a decrease in sphingomyelin (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myriocin treatment restored the levels of sphingolipid intermediates in VPS53 knock-down HeLa cells.
source: Importantly, myriocin treatment restored the levels of these sphingolipid intermediates in VPS53 knock-down cells (Figure 6D)
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PCCA2 fibroblasts exhibited increases in sphingosine, sphinganine, and ceramides compared with control fibroblasts.
source: Similar to VPS53 knock-down in HeLa cells, PCCA2 fibroblasts exhibited increases in sphingosine, sphinganine, and ceramides compared with control fibroblasts
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Myriocin treatment reduced the accumulation of sphingolipid intermediates in PCCA2 fibroblasts to levels similar to those found in untreated control fibroblasts.
source: Similar to what was observed for VPS53 knock-down in HeLa cells, myriocin treatment reduced the accumulation of sphingolipid intermediates in PCCA2 fibroblasts to levels similar to those found in untreated control fibroblasts (Figure 6E)
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In GARP mutants, membrane-derived lipids are rerouted to vacuoles (or lysosomes) for degradation.
source: In GARP mutants, however, some membrane-derived lipids appear to be rerouted to vacuoles (or lysosomes) for degradation
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of sphingolipid accumulation in vacuoles and increased long-chain bases in GARP mutants.

claim: The reduction in membrane sphingolipids may explain GARP's apparent role in plasma membrane organization.
source: This reduction in membrane sphingolipids may explain GARP's apparent role in plasma membrane organization, reported previously in genome-wide visual screens (Grossmann et al., 2008; Frohlich et al., 2009)
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to previous observations, supported by citations.

claim: In lysosomes, sphingolipids are broken down by acid sphingomyelinase and ceramidase, likely contributing to the elevation in sphingoid bases.
source: In lysosomes, sphingolipids are broken down by acid sphingomyelinase and ceramidase, likely contributing to the elevation in sphingoid bases
evidence: This is an inference based on known lysosomal sphingolipid metabolism and the observed accumulation of sphingoid bases.

claim: Missorting of sphingolipid synthesis enzymes or trafficking proteins in GARP mutants could contribute to the observed phenotypes.
source: However, it is also possible that missorting of sphingolipid synthesis enzymes or trafficking proteins in GARP mutants contributes to the observed phenotypes
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms that could contribute to the phenotypes.

claim: A protein important for the export of sphingolipid intermediates from lysosomes/vacuoles could be missorted in GARP mutants.
source: For instance, a protein important for the export of sphingolipid intermediates from lysosomes/vacuoles could be missorted in GARP mutants, thus increasing vacuolar sphingolipid accumulation
evidence: This is speculation about a specific mechanism that could explain the observed accumulation.

claim: The accumulation of early sphingolipid synthesis intermediates due to GARP deficiency may result in cellular toxicity.
source: Several of our findings suggest that the accumulation of early sphingolipid synthesis intermediates due to GARP deficiency may result in cellular toxicity
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations including growth defects and sensitivity to long-chain bases.

claim: Low levels of plasma membrane sphingolipids in GARP mutants activate TORC2/Slm/Ypk signaling.
source: Consistent with a decrease of plasma membrane sphingolipids, we found that the Orm1/2 proteins are hyperphosphorylated in GARP mutants suggesting that de novo sphingolipid synthesis is also upregulated
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed Orm1/2 hyperphosphorylation and established knowledge about the TORC2/Slm/Ypk signaling pathway.

claim: Long-chain bases possess detergent-like properties, especially in an acidic environment.
source: One possibility is that long-chain bases possess detergent-like properties, especially in an acidic environment (Jimenez-Rojo et al., 2014), such as in the yeast vacuole
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jimenez-Rojo et al., 2014.

claim: In model membranes such as giant unilamellar vesicles, long-chain bases lead to vesicular leakage.
source: In model membranes, such as giant unilamellar vesicles, this detergent-like action leads to vesicular leakage (Contreras et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Contreras et al., 2006.

claim: Long-chain bases inhibit glycerolipid synthesis.
source: Alternatively, long-chain bases are known to inhibit glycerolipid synthesis (Wu et al., 1993), which might contribute to their cytotoxicity
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 1993.

claim: Sphingolipids and sterols interact with each other in membranes.
source: Sphingolipids and sterols are thought to interact with each other in membranes
evidence: This represents established knowledge in membrane biology.

claim: In GARP mutants, sphingolipids are degraded in the lysosome/vacuole leading to a toxic build-up of sphingolipid metabolites, whereas sterols are exported and stored in cytoplasmic lipid droplets as more inert fatty acid esters.
source: Our data are most consistent with a model where sphingolipids are degraded in the lysosome/vacuole leading to a toxic build-up of sphingolipid metabolites, whereas sterols are exported and stored in cytoplasmic lipid droplets as more inert fatty acid esters
evidence: This is a model inferred from multiple experimental observations including lipid accumulation patterns and organelle phenotypes.

claim: Lowering sphingolipid levels by myriocin treatment of wild-type cells increases sterols stained by filipin.
source: Consistent with this, lowering sphingolipid levels by myriocin treatment of wild-type cells increases sterols stained by filipin
evidence: This is inferred from the filipin staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the absence of sufficient sphingolipids, sterols that are not complexed with sphingolipids build-up and are stored in ester form.
source: Possibly, this indicates that in the absence of sufficient sphingolipids, sterols that are not complexed with sphingolipids build-up and are stored in ester form
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed sterol accumulation.

claim: Accumulation of sphingolipid intermediates impairs normal sterol homeostasis in GARP mutants.
source: These data argue that in addition to sterol missorting in GARP mutants, accumulation of sphingolipid intermediates impairs normal sterol homeostasis, for example, by interfering with sterol export from the vacuole/lysosome or synthesis regulation
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that myriocin treatment suppresses sterol accumulation in GARP mutants.

claim: A primary cause for defects due to GARP deficiency may be lysosomal/vacuolar dysfunction due to sphingolipid accumulation.
source: This further highlights that a primary cause for defects due to GARP deficiency may be lysosomal/vacuolar dysfunction due to sphingolipid accumulation
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple experimental observations about vacuolar/lysosomal phenotypes and their suppression by myriocin.

claim: Mutations in VPS51, VPS53, and VPS54 are associated with neutral lipid accumulation in lipid droplets.
source: Consistent with our findings on sterol accumulation in GARP mutants, previous screens for lipid droplet phenotypes have identified mutations of several GARP subunit genes (VPS51, VPS53, and VPS54) to be associated with neutral lipid accumulation in LDs (Szymanski et al., 2007; Fei et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Szymanski et al., 2007 and Fei et al., 2008.

claim: Mutations in the zebrafish homolog of Vps51, fat-free, result in an increased number of lipid droplets in the liver and intestine.
source: In addition, mutations in the zebrafish homolog of Vps51, fat-free, result in an increased number of lipid droplets in the liver and intestine (Liu et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2010.

claim: VPS53 Q695R is one of two PCCA2 alleles.
source: The autosomal disease, linked thus far to two PCCA2 alleles, the missense Q695R mutation, and a splice donor mutation
evidence: This is stated as factual information about the disease alleles.

claim: VPS53 Q695R leads to defects in yeast that are similar to, albeit not as severe as, a Vps53 deletion.
source: Our data show that one of these mutations, VPS53 Q695R, leads to defects in yeast that are similar to, albeit not as severe as, a Vps53 deletion
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the vps53 Q624R mutant (analogous to human Q695R) to vps53Δ deletion.

claim: The pathogenesis of PCCA2 could be, at least partially, due to defects in lipid balance and storage.
source: Thus, the pathogenesis of PCCA2 could be, at least partially, due to defects in lipid balance and storage
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed sphingolipid imbalances in PCCA2 patient fibroblasts and their correction by myriocin.

claim: The disruption of the GARP subunit Vps54 in mice leads to a 'wobbler' phenotype, indicative of neurodegenerative disease sharing characteristics of ALS.
source: Interestingly, the disruption of the GARP subunit Vps54 in mice leads to a 'wobbler' phenotype, indicative of neurodegenerative disease sharing characteristics of ALS, including progressive motor degeneration and motor neuron loss (Perez-Victoria et al., 2010; Moser et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perez-Victoria et al., 2010 and Moser et al., 2013.

claim: Sphingolipid intermediates and sterol esters accumulate in ALS patients' brains.
source: Analyses of brain lipid profiles suggest sphingolipid intermediates and sterol esters accumulate in ALS patients (Cutler et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cutler et al., 2002.

claim: Mutations in the endo-lysosomal trafficking machinery (CHMP2B, FIG4, VAPB, and VCP) have been implicated in neurodegenerative disorders including ALS and FTD.
source: In addition, mutations in the endo-lysosomal trafficking machinery have been implicated in neurodegenerative disorders including ALS and FTD (CHMP2B, FIG4, VAPB, and VCP) (Yang et al., 2001; Parkinson et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2010; Maruyama et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2001; Parkinson et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2010; Maruyama et al., 2010.

claim: Defects in retrograde trafficking (VPS35) increase the risk for Parkinson's disease.
source: and defects in retrograde trafficking increase the risk for Parkinson's disease (VPS35) (Zimprich et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zimprich et al., 2011.

claim: Lipid imbalance and toxicity due to impaired endo-lysosomal trafficking could be a common feature of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Our data therefore suggest that lipid imbalance and toxicity due to impaired endo-lysosomal trafficking could be a common feature of this group of neurodegenerative diseases
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and the cited literature linking endo-lysosomal trafficking defects to various neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Inhibition of SPT may provide a useful therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases caused by impaired endo-lysosomal trafficking.
source: Since inhibition of SPT reversed some aspects of cellular dysfunction in our studies, our findings suggest that inhibition of the initial step of sphingolipid synthesis may provide a useful therapeutic strategy to pursue in these diseases
evidence: This is speculation about therapeutic applications based on the experimental findings that myriocin suppresses GARP deficiency phenotypes.
